name: Fenretinide

lead: Fenretinide is a synthetic retinoid that has been tested in cancer prevention, cancer treatment and retinal disease.
It is chemically related to the retinoids used for skin, which is why it comes up in appearance discussions, but published work does not cover skin appearance.

paras: Laboratory research describes effects on ceramide and sphingolipid pathways and on retinol-binding protein 4, a vitamin A carrier linked to insulin resistance.
It is investigational. Studies have looked at effects on retinal function, and it is not sold as a consumer skin product.

chain: Studied for cancer prevention and eye disease, not as a skin product
Appears in appearance discussion as a retinoid relative
angle.text: Fenretinide belongs to the same chemical family as skin retinoids, so it is sometimes mentioned in skin-focused discussions. Published work has examined it for cancer prevention and treatment and for retinal disease rather than for skin appearance.

lead: Fenretinide, also called 4-HPR or N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)retinamide, is a synthetic derivative of vitamin A in the retinoid family. It was developed and studied mainly as a cancer-prevention and anticancer drug, and has also been tested in eye disease and examined for effects on insulin sensitivity [1][2].

Its interest for appearance comes from its retinoid class: retinoids such as tretinoin and isotretinoin are widely used for skin. Fenretinide is not a marketed skin or cosmetic product, and its literature concerns oncology and ophthalmology rather than skin appearance.

In human studies it has been given by mouth to women at risk of breast cancer, to people with oral leukoplakia and to children and adults with tumours, and newer formulations such as intravenous emulsions and nanoparticle forms are in trials [3][4][5][6].
infobox: Oral; intravenous emulsion in some trials
Cancer prevention and treatment, retinal disease, insulin resistance
Investigational; not a marketed skin product

paras: Fenretinide has no established cosmetic or dermatological use. It appears in appearance-oriented discussion mainly as a retinoid relative, with interest following that of tretinoin and isotretinoin.

Fenretinide is investigational. It has been tested for cancer chemoprevention, including a randomised trial of 2,972 women with early breast cancer or ductal carcinoma in situ who received it orally or no treatment for five years to look at second breast malignancy [3], and trials in oral leukoplakia, ovarian cancer occurrence and basal cell carcinoma [7][4].

Laboratory work describes fenretinide as acting partly through ceramide and sphingolipid pathways, with ceramide increases and cell death in neuroblastoma cell lines [8][9]. It also lowers circulating retinol-binding protein 4, which has been linked to insulin resistance in obesity and type 2 diabetes in animal and human data [1], and it has been studied in the retinal visual cycle [10].

Because it interacts with vitamin A transport and retinal pathways, eye effects have been studied. An electroretinogram study of 24 women treated for a median of 30.5 months compared them with 18 untreated controls in a phase III trial [11], and reviews list retinal toxicities among systemic anticancer drug effects [12].

Fenretinide is a research compound and is not sold as a consumer skin product. It is occasionally raised in appearance communities as a retinoid with possible relevance to skin, fat and insulin sensitivity, though discussion is limited.

Human trials have studied fenretinide in breast cancer prevention, oral leukoplakia, ovarian cancer occurrence, head and neck cancer, neuroblastoma and other solid tumours, lymphoma, and geographic atrophy in dry age-related macular degeneration [3][7][4][13][2][6]. A phase 1 study in healthy volunteers and a phase 1 trial of a nanoparticle formulation in small cell lung cancer are registered [14][5]. No trial has tested fenretinide for skin appearance.

Current work includes new formulations such as intravenous emulsions and nanofenretinide, and studies of its sphingolipid effects [5][6][9]. Reviews describe it as having roles across cancer and neurological or retinal disease.

timeline.event: Controlled trials in breast cancer, basal cell carcinoma and oral leukoplakia are reviewed.
Randomised trial of fenretinide for second breast malignancy reported [3].
RBP4 linked to insulin resistance, with fenretinide as a RBP4-lowering agent [1].
Trial in geographic atrophy of dry macular degeneration begins [2].
